strengths: The proposed combination of time-conditioned adversarial marginal matching and conditional flow matching is well motivated. The endpoint-preserving interpolant parameterization provides a practical way to incorporate intermediate observations without prescribing sample-level correspondences.
The knot and cell-segmentation examples provide compelling qualitative illustrations of learning smooth trajectories from sparsely sampled, time-varying distributions.

The spatial transcriptomics experiment reports improved held-out EMD: 98.91 versus 109.17 for the strongest reported baseline. Experiments span several applications and dimensions, and the appendix provides useful dataset and architecture details.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 has a substantive feasibility gap. Its proposed optimizer, G = T composed with the piecewise reference, depends on the intermediate sample, whereas the admissible G receives only the endpoints and time. A Markov-chained OT coupling does not generally make the intermediate sample a deterministic function of the endpoints. Indeed, both endpoint distributions can be point masses while the intermediate distribution and reference distribution are absolutely continuous; no deterministic endpoint-conditioned G can then generate a nondegenerate target. The stated assumptions therefore do not guarantee existence or uniqueness.

The uniqueness claims exceed what the theory establishes. Theorem 2.1 concerns a fixed-time, exactly constrained transport problem, not the finite-weight adversarial objective actually optimized. Uniqueness at observed times also does not establish unique trajectories between observations. Its proof additionally writes G = T composed with the reference minus the reference, although the interpolant should be T composed with the reference. Equation (12) is incorrect as written: its second branch does not recover x1 at t = 1. These issues require correction and a clearer separation between theoretical guarantees and practical training.

The claim of matching state-of-the-art single-cell performance is not supported consistently. OT-MFM outperforms ALI-CFM in every setting in Tables 1–2. On 100D Cite, the respective EMDs are 42.232 and 48.496; ALI-CFM also underperforms ordinary OT-CFM there. The explanation that adversarial distribution matching loses on a 'pointwise' metric is unconvincing because EMD is itself a distributional metric evaluated on held-out marginals.

The strongest qualitative claims lack quantitative validation. The synthetic and cell-tracking studies provide no EMD, tracking-error, smoothness, or repeated-run comparisons, despite available reference distributions or segmentation masks. Cell tracking uses only one cell sequence. Omitting the spline baseline because it behaved similarly on a different synthetic task is insufficient, and attributing baseline failures to interpolant kinks or loss variance requires direct measurements and training or solver diagnostics.

Baseline coverage and fidelity limit the conclusions. The MMFM implementation removes its Gaussian probability path, and high-dimensional MMFM experiments are omitted on scalability grounds without measured runtime or memory evidence. The principal MFM comparisons emphasize a time-independent metric, while a multi-marginal variant is excluded from the spatial experiment without numerical results. These choices weaken claims of superiority over existing multi-marginal methods.

There are no controlled ablations separating adversarial matching from regularization, pretraining, coupling, time-input noise, and metric choice. This is particularly important because the single-cell implementation changes to R3GAN and a LAND-weighted second-derivative penalty. Comparisons with regularizer-only training and alternative distribution-matching losses are needed to establish which component provides the benefit.

The spatial transcriptomics evidence is narrow: four sections from one dataset yield only two held-out interpolation tasks. Manual alignment includes the held-out sections, so the evaluation should clarify its dependence on held-out histology and registration information. Per-section results, the meaning of the reported uncertainty, and broader replication are needed. Scalability and reproducibility are also incompletely supported: training costs are unreported, and details such as the finite-difference step and final regularization settings are insufficiently specified.

strengths: The proposed combination of endpoint-preserving neural interpolants, adversarial matching of intermediate marginals, and subsequent conditional flow matching is coherent and potentially useful for noisy, densely sampled temporal data.
The knot and cell-tracking visualizations illustrate promising behavior when the data geometry changes over time.

On spatial transcriptomics, ALI-CFM achieves the lowest reported EMD: 98.91 versus approximately 109 for CFM and MMFM. The paper also evaluates several single-cell datasets and provides substantial architectural and training details.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 is false under its stated assumptions. Its proof constructs G = T composed with a reference depending on the intermediate sample, although G may depend only on the endpoints and time. For example, take both endpoint distributions to be a point mass at zero and the intermediate distribution to be uniform on an interval. The Markov-chained pairwise OT coupling satisfies the reference absolute-continuity assumption at the intermediate time, but a deterministic function of the constant endpoints cannot generate the required uniform marginal. Thus even existence fails.

The broader claim of unique interpolant trajectories is unsupported. Theorem 2.1 concerns a fixed-time, exactly constrained transport problem; it does not establish uniqueness for the finite-weight adversarial objective, neural parameterization, or paths between observed times. Smooth perturbations vanishing at every observed timestamp leave both the adversarial loss and the linear-reference regularizer unchanged. The proof also incorrectly writes the optimizer as T composed with the reference minus the reference, rather than T composed with the reference.

The claim of performance 'on par' with state-of-the-art single-cell methods overstates Tables 1–2. OT-MFM has lower EMD in all seven reported dataset/dimension settings. On Cite, ALI-CFM scores 41.449 versus 36.471 at 50 dimensions and 48.496 versus 42.232 at 100 dimensions, and also underperforms OT-CFM. The explanation invoking a disadvantage on 'pointwise metrics' is unconvincing because held-out EMD measures distributional discrepancy.

The strongest claimed advantages on knot and cell-tracking data lack quantitative evaluation, repeated-run uncertainty, and controlled noise or sample-size studies. Cell tracking uses only one cell sequence, and the authors explicitly restrict evaluation to visual inspection. Claims that baseline divergence is caused by interpolation kinks or high gradient variance are not supported by measured variance, solver-sensitivity experiments, or matched-compute studies.

Baseline coverage and fidelity limit the conclusions. MMFM is reimplemented without its Gaussian probability path, excluded from higher-dimensional experiments without measured scaling evidence, and omitted from cell tracking based on a different experiment. The comparisons do not establish whether smoothing splines or temporal adaptations of metric-based methods would resolve the highlighted failures.

There are no controlled ablations isolating adversarial matching from reference regression, pretraining, time-input noise, coupling, and regularization. The single-cell implementation additionally uses R3GAN and a LAND-weighted regularizer, making attribution especially difficult. Runtime, memory, and training-stability measurements are missing despite scalability claims and substantial additional interpolant training.

The spatial-transcriptomics evidence is narrow: four sections from one dataset, with only two interior sections held out. Manual nonlinear registration includes the held-out histology, so the experiment assesses coordinate interpolation conditional on that preprocessing rather than reconstruction of a wholly unobserved section. Per-section results, uncertainty definitions, registration sensitivity, and additional specimens are needed to substantiate broad application claims.

strengths: The proposed combination of time-conditioned adversarial distribution matching and conditional flow matching is conceptually appealing. The endpoint-preserving parametrisation provides a practical way to learn flexible interpolants from unpaired snapshots.
The synthetic knot and cell-tracking visualisations show promising behaviour with many sparsely sampled marginals and changing spatial geometry.
The spatial transcriptomics experiment reports an encouraging improvement: EMD decreases from 109.17 for OT-MMFM to 98.91 for OT-ALI-CFM, with lower reported variability.

The evaluation covers several application settings and dimensions up to 100. Dataset links, architectural choices, and substantial training details are provided, and the single-cell experiments include five independent runs.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 has a substantive feasibility gap. Its proof constructs G = T composed with a reference that depends on the intermediate sample, although G may depend only on the endpoints. Absolute continuity of the reference does not resolve this. For example, both endpoint distributions can be point masses while the intermediate distribution is Gaussian: the Markov-chained OT reference is absolutely continuous at the intermediate time, but a deterministic function of the fixed endpoints cannot generate that Gaussian. Additional assumptions and a different argument are needed.

The claimed uniqueness of smooth trajectories exceeds the theoretical results. Theorem 2.1 concerns a fixed-time, exactly constrained optimisation problem; it does not establish uniqueness between observed timestamps or for the finite-weight adversarial objective actually trained. Smooth perturbations that vanish at observed times leave the linear-reference training objective unchanged. Its proof also incorrectly writes G = T composed with the linear reference minus the reference, rather than simply G = T composed with the reference.

Equation (12) is not a valid piecewise linear interpolant as written: the second branch evaluates to x1/(1-ti) at t=1, rather than x1, and the first branch uses an unexplained tk. Because this regulariser supports the strongest quantitative result, clarifying the implemented formula is important.

The claim of performance 'on par' with state-of-the-art single-cell methods is not supported consistently. OT-MFM has lower mean EMD in all seven reported settings. On 100D Cite, the scores are 48.496 versus 42.232, and on 50D Cite they are 41.449 versus 36.471. The explanation invoking a disadvantage on 'pointwise metrics' is unconvincing: EMD compares distributions, and the evaluated marginals are held out.

The strongest qualitative claims lack quantitative validation. The knot experiment and tracking of a single cell provide no distributional-error, smoothness, or repeated-run results. Baseline divergence is not investigated through solver or optimisation controls. The spatial transcriptomics evidence comes from only four sections of one specimen, with two held-out sections; this is insufficient to establish broad superiority or statistical significance.

Baseline coverage and fidelity limit the comparisons. MMFM is reimplemented without its Gaussian probability path, omitted from high-dimensional experiments without measured scaling evidence, and excluded from cell tracking based on a different experiment. The assertion that cubic splines exhibit kinks also needs correction or qualification: standard cubic splines are smooth, although noisy data can produce large derivatives.

There are no controlled ablations isolating adversarial matching from regularisation, pretraining, coupling, and time-input noise. The final single-cell method additionally uses a time-dependent LAND metric, making attribution especially important. Runtime and memory comparisons are missing, and some consequential settings, including the finite-difference step and precise regulariser scaling, are insufficiently specified.

strengths: The proposed combination of endpoint-preserving neural interpolants, adversarial intermediate-marginal matching, and conditional flow matching is conceptually appealing and addresses a relevant problem with unpaired snapshots.

The knot and cell-mask experiments provide promising visual evidence that learning distributions jointly across time can improve robustness to sparse sampling compared with the evaluated piecewise interpolation baselines.

The spatial transcriptomics experiment reports an encouraging EMD improvement: 98.91 versus 109.17 for the strongest baseline. The paper also includes multiple single-cell datasets, repeated runs, regularizer ablations, and substantial implementation details.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 is false under its stated assumptions. Its proposed optimizer in Equation (20) depends on the intermediate sample, although G may depend only on the endpoints and time. For a concrete counterexample, let both endpoint distributions be point masses at zero and the intermediate distribution be uniform. The Markov-chained OT coupling exists and its reference distribution at the intermediate time is absolutely continuous, but any deterministic endpoint-conditioned G is constant and cannot match the uniform target. Thus even existence fails.

The theoretical results do not establish the advertised uniqueness of learned trajectories. Theorem 2.1 concerns a fixed-time, exactly constrained optimization problem, whereas training uses a finite-weight adversarial penalty and observes only discrete times. Unique values at observed times do not determine a unique smooth trajectory between them. There are additional formula errors: the optimizer in the proof of Theorem 2.1 should be T composed with the reference, without subtracting the reference; Equation (12)'s second branch does not satisfy the intended endpoint conditions.

The claim of performance 'on par' with state-of-the-art single-cell methods is not supported by Tables 1–2. OT-MFM outperforms ALI-CFM in every reported setting. For Cite, EMD increases from 36.471 to 41.449 in 50D and from 42.232 to 48.496 in 100D, differences substantially larger than the reported variability. EMD is a distributional metric, so attributing these differences to competing methods overfitting a 'pointwise metric' is unconvincing.

The strongest demonstrations of robustness rely on visual evaluation of one synthetic construction and one tracked cell. Despite available full masks and known synthetic distributions, there are no quantitative distribution errors, repeated-subsampling statistics, or systematic noise sweeps. Baseline divergence alone does not establish the proposed explanation involving gradient variance or general superiority across changing geometries.

Comparisons and ablations do not isolate the adversarial contribution. Missing controls include the same neural interpolant trained with regularization alone, non-adversarial distribution-matching losses, and smoothing baselines. MMFM is modified by removing its Gaussian probability path and excluded from higher-dimensional experiments; the cited high-dimensional method of Lee et al. is not evaluated. These choices weaken broad claims about competing methods.

The spatial transcriptomics evidence is narrow: four sections from one dataset and two held-out positions. Registration uses manually selected landmarks from all sections, including held-out images, so the experiment assumes access to held-out morphology and does not establish prediction for a wholly unobserved section. Per-section results, clearer uncertainty reporting, and independent tissues are needed to substantiate the claimed significant advantage.

Reproducibility and scalability evidence remain incomplete. The strongest single-cell configuration uses R3GAN and a LAND-based regularizer rather than the main presentation's standard GAN objective, without fully specifying the resulting loss and selection procedure. The finite-difference step size is unspecified, and there is no systematic end-to-end runtime or memory comparison supporting scalability claims.

strengths: The method offers a useful combination of adversarial intermediate-marginal matching and conditional flow matching, with endpoint constraints enforced by construction.
The knot and cell-motion examples show promising qualitative improvements when many sparsely sampled marginals make conventional interpolants difficult to fit.

The spatial transcriptomics experiment reports the best average EMD: 98.91 versus 109.17 for the strongest reported baseline. The appendix provides substantial implementation details and regularisation ablations.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 has a substantive feasibility gap. Its proposed optimizer in Eq. (20) depends on the intermediate sample, although G may depend only on the endpoints and time. The stated assumptions do not make that intermediate sample recoverable from the endpoints. For example, point-mass endpoints and an absolutely continuous intermediate marginal satisfy the reference-distribution assumption at the intermediate time, but a deterministic endpoint-conditioned G cannot generate that marginal.

The uniqueness claims exceed the theoretical results. Theorems concern exact marginal constraints at fixed times, whereas training uses a finite-weight adversarial penalty and restricted neural networks. Uniqueness at observed times also does not establish unique trajectories between them. Theorem 2.1's proof additionally gives G = T composed with the reference minus the reference, which describes a correction rather than the claimed interpolant.

Equation (12) incorrectly defines the second piece of the piecewise-linear reference: its endpoint coefficients do not yield x1 at t = 1 or continuity at the intermediate time. Whether the implementation uses the correct expression is unclear.

The claim of performance 'on par' with state of the art is inadequately supported. OT-MFM has lower EMD in every setting in Tables 1–2. On Cite, ALI-CFM is approximately 14% worse at 50 dimensions and 15% worse at 100 dimensions, and also underperforms ordinary OT-CFM. Explaining these gaps through 'pointwise metrics' is misleading because EMD measures distributional discrepancy on held-out marginals.

The strongest qualitative claims lack quantitative validation. The cell experiment uses one cell sequence and explicitly omits numerical evaluation despite having full segmentation masks. Distributional errors, centroid errors, repeated subsampling, and solver sensitivity would help distinguish a robust methodological advantage from particular baseline failures.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of adversarial training from smoothing, pretraining, and regularisation. Missing controls include regularisation-only training, non-adversarial distribution-matching objectives, and smoothing-spline baselines. MMFM is modified by removing its Gaussian probability path, while the cited high-dimensional method of Lee et al. is not evaluated.

The spatial transcriptomics evidence is limited to four sections from one dataset, with two held-out interpolation targets and manual nonlinear registration. Per-section results, a clear account of uncertainty, registration sensitivity, and additional specimens are needed to support broad superiority claims. Likewise, scalability claims lack systematic runtime and memory comparisons.

strengths: ALI-CFM offers a useful approach to multi-marginal flow matching: learn endpoint-preserving neural interpolants through adversarial matching of intermediate distributions, then distill their velocities through conditional flow matching. This directly addresses noisy, sparsely sampled marginals without requiring interpolation through every observed sample.

The knot and cell-tracking visualizations provide encouraging evidence that globally learned interpolants can avoid instability encountered by the tested piecewise interpolation baselines when there are many observation times.

The spatial transcriptomics experiment reports improved EMD: 98.91±2.03 versus 109.17±9.82 for OT-MMFM and 109.76±9.98 for OT-CFM. The paper also includes multiple single-cell datasets, repeated runs, regularizer studies, and substantial implementation details.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 is false under its stated assumptions. Its proposed optimizer, T composed with the piecewise reference, depends on the intermediate sample, whereas the admissible generator only receives the endpoints and time. For example, let both endpoint distributions be point masses at zero and the intermediate distribution be continuous. The chained OT coupling exists and the reference distribution at the intermediate time is absolutely continuous, but any deterministic endpoint-conditioned generator is constant and cannot match that distribution. The proof therefore does not establish even existence, let alone uniqueness.

The broader claim of unique learned trajectories is unsupported. Theorems about exact marginal constraints at a fixed time do not establish uniqueness for the finite-weight adversarial objective, its neural parameterization, or trajectories between finitely many observed times. Theorem 2.1 also incorrectly writes its optimizer as T composed with the linear reference minus that reference; the subtraction should not appear for G as defined. Equation (12)'s second branch fails to recover x1 at t=1, leaving the implemented regularizer unclear.

The claim of performance 'on par' with state-of-the-art single-cell methods is overstated. OT-MFM has lower mean EMD in all seven settings in Tables 1–2. On Cite, ALI-CFM obtains 41.449 versus 36.471 in 50D and 48.496 versus 42.232 in 100D, gaps substantially larger than the reported variability; it also trails OT-CFM in these settings. Explaining this through EMD being a pointwise metric is unconvincing: EMD measures distributional discrepancy, and these evaluations use held-out marginals.

The strongest claims about noisy-data robustness and large numbers of marginals rely on qualitative evaluation of one synthetic construction and one tracked cell. Quantitative marginal error, repeated subsampling, controlled noise sweeps, and measured gradient variance are missing. Baseline divergence alone does not establish that piecewise interpolation intrinsically causes failure; solver accuracy, temporal resolution, and training-budget controls would strengthen that conclusion.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of adversarial matching. There is no clear regularizer-only or no-adversarial-loss baseline, nor a comparison against another distribution-matching loss. Practical single-cell training additionally uses R3GAN, pretraining, time jitter, and a LAND-based regularizer, so the contribution of the proposed adversarial mechanism remains uncertain. MMFM is modified by removing its Gaussian probability path and omitted at higher dimensions without a systematic accuracy–runtime comparison.

The spatial transcriptomics result is promising but narrow: four sections from one dataset and two held-out-section settings. All sections undergo manual image-based registration, including held-out sections, so the demonstrated task is coordinate interpolation after access to their histology rather than fully unobserved-section reconstruction. Additional specimens, registration-sensitivity analysis, and clearer uncertainty reporting are needed to support the claimed general significance.
